title: Module 2: Enterprise Integration & Production
description: Take a designed solution from proof of concept to enterprise-ready production: cost, latency, reliability, and integration patterns.

questions.question: When moving a Claude-based solution from PoC to production, which metric should an architect prioritize first?
options: Number of API calls per day
Mapping cost, latency, and reliability targets to the enterprise's budget and SLAs
Total number of users
Length of the system prompt
questions.explanation: Production readiness requires mapping concrete cost, latency, and reliability targets to the enterprise's budget and service-level agreements before scaling.

questions.question: Which integration pattern is most appropriate for embedding Claude capabilities into an existing enterprise workflow with strict security policies?
options: Direct user access to Claude's web UI
API-based integration with authentication, rate limiting, and audit logging
Copying and pasting results between systems
Running Claude locally on a developer's laptop
questions.explanation: API-based integration with auth, rate limiting, and audit logging provides the security controls and observability that enterprises require for production.

questions.question: In a production Claude deployment, what is the recommended strategy for handling API rate limits?
options: Ignore them and let failures occur organically
Implement request queuing, backpressure, and client-side rate limiting with fallback responses
Use a single API key across all services
Reduce the prompt size to zero
questions.explanation: Production systems need queuing, backpressure, and client-side rate management to handle capacity constraints gracefully without dropping user requests.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of implementing caching in a Claude-based production system?
options: To eliminate the need for the Claude API entirely
To reduce latency and cost by serving previously computed responses for repeated or similar queries
To increase the complexity of the architecture
To store user credentials
questions.explanation: Caching (including prompt caching and response caching) reduces both latency and cost by avoiding redundant API calls for repeated queries.

questions.question: When designing for high availability in a Claude-based system, which pattern should an architect implement?
options: A single-point deployment with no redundancy
Graceful degradation: the system continues operating with reduced capability when Claude is unavailable
Always rely on Claude without any fallback
Disable all non-essential features during outages
questions.explanation: Graceful degradation ensures the system remains partially functional even during Claude API outages, falling back to cached responses or simplified workflows.

questions.question: Which of the following is a critical consideration for data residency in a Claude enterprise deployment?
options: Data residency does not matter for cloud-based AI
Customer data may need to remain in specific geographic regions; the architecture must enforce this at the integration layer
All data must be stored in Claude's servers permanently
Only anonymized data can be sent to Claude
questions.explanation: Enterprise deployments must respect data residency requirements (e.g., GDPR, regional laws), enforcing data location constraints at the integration layer.

questions.question: What is the role of observability in a production Claude system?
options: It is optional and only useful during development
It provides real-time visibility into cost, latency, error rates, and usage patterns to drive operational decisions
It replaces the need for security controls
It only tracks user login times
questions.explanation: Observability (monitoring, logging, alerting) is essential for production Claude systems to track performance, cost, and reliability in real time.

questions.question: When scaling a Claude-based service, which approach balances cost and performance most effectively?
options: Always use the largest, most capable model for every request
Route simple tasks to smaller/faster models and complex reasoning tasks to larger models
Use only the smallest model to minimize cost
Run all models in parallel for every request
questions.explanation: Model routing (tiered model selection) assigns tasks to the most appropriate model based on complexity, optimizing both cost and performance.

questions.question: What is a key challenge when integrating Claude with legacy enterprise systems?
options: Legacy systems are always faster than Claude
Bridging asynchronous, event-driven Claude workflows with synchronous, batch-oriented legacy systems requires careful adapter design
Legacy systems never require integration
Claude cannot interact with any external system
questions.explanation: Legacy systems often use synchronous batch processing, while Claude operates asynchronously with tool calls, requiring careful adapter and queue design.

questions.question: Which pattern is recommended for managing configuration in a multi-environment (dev/staging/prod) Claude deployment?
options: Hardcode all configuration in the source code
Use environment-specific configuration files or a configuration service, never hardcode credentials or endpoints
Share the same configuration across all environments
Store configuration only in the system prompt
questions.explanation: Environment-specific configuration (via config files, secrets managers, or config services) allows safe deployment across dev, staging, and production.

questions.question: What is the purpose of implementing circuit breakers in a Claude-based production system?
options: To increase the number of API calls
To prevent cascading failures by temporarily stopping requests to Claude when error rates exceed a threshold
To cache all responses indefinitely
To replace the need for monitoring
questions.explanation: Circuit breakers detect elevated error rates and temporarily halt requests, preventing cascading failures and allowing the system to recover.

questions.question: In a production Claude deployment, how should an architect approach cost management?
options: Cost is not a concern in production
Implement token budgeting, per-tenant cost tracking, and alerting on cost anomalies
Only track total monthly spend
Let the cloud provider handle all cost optimization
questions.explanation: Production cost management requires granular tracking (per-tenant, per-feature), budgeting, and anomaly detection to prevent cost overruns.

questions.question: What is the recommended approach for handling sensitive data in Claude API requests?
options: Send all data without filtering
Apply PII detection and redaction before sending data to Claude, and avoid storing sensitive data in logs
Only anonymize data in development
Encrypt data only at rest
questions.explanation: PII detection, redaction, and careful log management are essential to prevent sensitive data from being exposed in API requests or logs.

questions.question: Which deployment strategy minimizes risk when rolling out a Claude-based feature to a large enterprise?
options: Big-bang release to all users simultaneously
Phased rollout with canary deployment, feature flags, and rollback capability
Deploy only during business hours
Skip staging and deploy directly to production
questions.explanation: Phased rollouts with canary deployments, feature flags, and easy rollback minimize blast radius and allow controlled validation in production.

questions.question: What is the role of a message queue (e.g., SQS, Kafka) in a Claude-based enterprise integration?
options: It replaces the Claude API
It decouples request ingestion from processing, enabling asynchronous handling of Claude interactions and backpressure management
It stores the model weights
It is only used for logging
questions.explanation: Message queues decouple ingestion from processing, enabling asynchronous, scalable handling of Claude interactions with built-in backpressure.
